content:
The lemma ContinuousOn.mul is tagged with to_fun and fun_prop, and so one gets two versions for fun_prop to use (as well as a to_additive version, but this is irrelevant for my post):

theorem ContinuousOn.mul {M : Type u_1} [TopologicalSpace M] [Mul M] [ContinuousMul M] {X : Type u_2} [TopologicalSpace X] {f g : X → M} {s : Set X} (hf : ContinuousOn f s) (hg : ContinuousOn g s) :
ContinuousOn (f * g) s

theorem ContinuousOn.fun_mul {M : Type u_1} [TopologicalSpace M] [Mul M] [ContinuousMul M] {X : Type u_2} [TopologicalSpace X] {f g : X → M} {s : Set X} (hf : ContinuousOn f s) (hg : ContinuousOn g s) :
ContinuousOn (fun (i : X) => f i * g i) s

On the other hand, ContinuousOn.inv is tagged with fun_prop but not to_fun, so one only gets one version:

theorem ContinuousOn.inv {G : Type u_1} {X : Type u_3} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace G] [Inv G] [ContinuousInv G] {f : X → G} {s : Set X} (hf : ContinuousOn f s) :
ContinuousOn (fun (x : X) => (f x)⁻¹) s

In particular, fun_prop cannot currently reduce expressions such as ContinuousOn (f ⁻¹ * g) s (or ContinuousOn (-f + g) s in the additive setting) because only one of the two needed fun_prop lemmas are available. There are many other examples like this for various other function properties and operations.

Would it make sense to systematically go through all the fun_prop lemmas and tag as many of them as possible with to_fun? This would increase the power of fun_prop. Unfortunately, it is also a large refactor because many lemmas would now change, e.g.,

theorem ContinuousOn.inv {G : Type u_1} {X : Type u_3} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace G] [Inv G] [ContinuousInv G] {f : X → G} {s : Set X} (hf : ContinuousOn f s) :
ContinuousOn f ⁻¹ s

theorem ContinuousOn.fun_inv {G : Type u_1} {X : Type u_3} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace G] [Inv G] [ContinuousInv G] {f : X → G} {s : Set X} (hf : ContinuousOn f s) :
ContinuousOn (fun (x : X) => (f x)⁻¹) s

though I guess what happens in practice is that many invocations of these theorems get replaced by their fun_ analogues.
Hello, I would agree to do such a refactor yes, but my knowledge of mathlib4 is quite limited here I should say. (I mostly used Rocq)
some related posts: #mathlib4 > Using fun_prop for the sum of two continuous functions, #mathlib4 > Convention for `f * g` and / or `fun x ↦ f x * g x`

It may also be possible to modify the meta code to maybe avoid a full refactor that way, would require some nuanced consideration though, as those other threads show.

It is perhaps partly a question stemming from the limitations of fun_prop , so tagging as many as possible in this sense may end up surfacing the potential patterns for changes in the meta code (implicit in the choice process for which to tag or not to tag).

In this case though, inverses are a little bit tricky in general given you can hunt for either side of the bijection and you have something like f = f⁻¹⁻¹ , so have to be careful to avoid any looping issues ( might be wrong about this , but have seen it before).

Currently doesn't seem like that shape gets this tag much if at all.

It is a fairly general tactic , so over time "edge cases" surface that sometimes just require straightforward tactic changes ( like #mathlib4 > `fun_prop` in `FunLike` with multiple arguments ).

#35306 and #33671 may be of some relevance.
Note that the to_fun exercise would have some value even outside of fun_prop; for instance currently the non-eta-expanded version of ContinuousOn.inv does not exist as a Mathlib theorem.

The missing to_fun on ContinuousOn.inv is clearly an oversight, and should be fixed (as all the other similar results). The reason is that these lemmas predate to_fun, and when we introduced to_fun we tagged the lemmas we noticed, but apparently we forgot a bunch of them!

I used an AI agent to collect instances where adding a to_fun tag (and, in some cases, converting the eta-expanded lemma to a point-free lemma) could be appropriate. Here is a table of "clean candidates" according to the AI:

Operation Family Location

inv₀ (f⁻¹, GroupWithZero) Continuous{,At,On}.inv₀ Topology/Algebra/GroupWithZero.lean:119,124,128
div' (f / g) Continuous{,At,On}.div' Topology/Algebra/Group/Defs.lean:147,157,161
pow (f ^ n) Continuous{,At,On}.pow Topology/Algebra/Monoid.lean:812,834,839
zpow (f ^ z) Continuous{,At,On}.zpow Topology/Algebra/Group/Basic.lean:478,500,505
smul (f • g) Continuous{WithinAt,At,On,}.smul Topology/Algebra/MulAction.lean:120,125,130,134
const_smul (c • f) Continuous{,At,On}.const_smul Topology/Algebra/ConstMulAction.lean:100,105,109
inv (f⁻¹) ContDiff{WithinAt,On,At,}.inv Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/Operations.lean:799,804,808,813
mul,div,inv,pow,smul Measurable/AEMeasurable.* MeasureTheory/Group/Arithmetic.lean (many)

smul (f • g) (AE)StronglyMeasurable.smul …/StronglyMeasurable/{Basic,AEStronglyMeasurable}.lean

There was an additional category where the point-free and eta-expanded versions existed separately without using to_fun; they could still be merged into a single to_fun lemma, but this probably requires manual attention. Here is the list (also AI-generated):

  • Topology: Continuous{,At,On}.div (point-free) ↔ .div₀ (eta), Topology/Algebra/GroupWithZero.lean
  • Calculus: Differentiable{,At,On}.div ↔ .fun_div, Analysis/Calculus/Deriv/Inv.lean:187–212
  • MeasureTheory: mul'/mul, div'/div, sup'/sup, inf'/inf, const_smul/const_smul', Integrable.sub/sub', Integrable.const_mul/const_mul', mul_const/mul_const' — across Group/Arithmetic.lean, Order/Lattice.lean, StronglyMeasurable/*, L1Space/Integrable.lean

I think I could pretty reliably get an AI agent to make the relevant changes in the first table as a PR, but perhaps it would be better if someone with a deeper understanding of global Mathlib structure performed this somewhat large refactor.

(There is also the downstream task of looking within Mathlib for places where fun_prop type arguments are currently done by hand and would now benefit from the increased fun_prop power provided by the above refactor, but perhaps this is low priority.)

I have two questions:

  • I'm not sure if the refactor might be too big to do at once. Especially for the to_fun parts?
  • Also I'm not sure about the table generated by the AI agent, it might be confabulating from there?

As long as it is a straight forward refactor, it doesn't matter if it is a bit big. The different kinds of refactor (using to_fun for generating new theorems vs for generating theorems that were already declared manually) should be done separately though.

Unfortunately there are few candidates for purely generating new theorems: in the situations where only one version of the theorem exists, it is usually the eta-expanded one, so if one were to install to_fun one would first have to change the eta-expanded lemma to the point-free form, apply to_fun, and then go through all downstream applications of the lemma and replace them with their fun_ versions (though if they were used via fun_prop this should happen automatically). But I think this could be done in a safe automated way with modern AI tools used responsibly.

Regarding the possibility of confabulation, the AI agent generated deterministic bash scripts which it then ran on my local Mathlib fork (and then inspected) to generate the above tables. Any given entry can be inspected manually: to pick one at random, docs#ContinuousAt.const_smul indeed only exists in eta-expanded form at the indicated line number 100.

Terence Tao said:

one would first have to change the eta-expanded lemma to the point-free form, apply to_fun, and then go through all downstream applications of the lemma and replace them with their fun_ versions

Yes, this is what should be done. I don't think the downstream fallout will be too bad to fix manually, because the two versions of the theorem are defeq to eachother (just not reducibly defeq). And in places where proofs do break, we can also choose to replace the proofs with fun_prop, to avoid mentioning the name of the theorem at all.

OK. I will wait to hear from other Mathlib experts first, but if it looks like there is agreement that one should refactor the lemmas in the first table, I can work with my AI agent to generate an appropriate PR (which will touch a large number of files, but in a fairly systematic way).

Such a PR would definitely be welcome! I don't care if it is AI generated or not, because it is very mechanical, there is no design decision to be made here (the old way to do such a refactor would be old-gen AI, i.e., regexp search and replace, and that's not so different). It is always a good idea to have a human look at the outcome, though, to check that everything looks reasonable.
OK, I will get started on this, with plenty of human-in-the-loop review at each stage of the process of course.

I thought we didn't want to auto-generate an eta-expanded version of every theorem, even if it's easily possible now. I even think you said so, @Sébastien Gouëzel --- so I'm curious what caused your change of minds.

I'm all for adding the expanded version when we need them, but I'm not sure whether we do.

Actually, the intended PR (targeting the table above) is doing the opposite: for every entry in this table, Mathlib only has the eta-expanded version, and not the point-free version. The refactor makes the point-free version available, but does not add any new eta-expanded theorems.
The reason for doing this refactor is that it makes fun_prop stronger.
Would it be better to get the AI to generate the regexp rather than to just let it do everything itself?
Using an AI agent to generate a regular expression would be promising yes, that would help us reproduce more steps accross agents.

It's not a pure regexp task. To create the table, the AI first did some regexp greps to locate candidates, and then did its LLM thing to decide which candidates were actually viable.

I'm two thirds of the way right now through a PR doing the refactor, mostly for the Topology and Calculus refactors (the MeasureTheory refactor is more of a notational mess, deferring it to later). Here there are some subtle issues that have emerged on case-by-case analysis. For instance, Differentiable.div and Differentiable.fun_div are already in Mathlib, with the expected spelling, so one should just delete Differentiable.fun_div and to_fun Differentiable.div, right? But Mathlib proves Differentiable.fun_div first and deduces Differentiable.div as a corollary, so the AI had to rearrange that.

The AI was able to fix most downstream usages by replacing for instance .inv with .fun_inv whenever the build broke, although the process I used of doing the refactors in batches created some temporary edge failure modes when multiple eta-expanded theorems were chained together, and the AI only performed the required renaming on some subset of these theorems, leading to temporary unification breakage.

I'll ask the AI to generate a detailed report which I will attach as a comment to the PR. Unfortunately it is going to be more complex than "just run this bash script".

so one should just delete Differentiable.fun_div and to_fun Differentiable.div, right?

Yes! (Assuming it is not too hard to do.)

Already done. The LLM is moving faster than lake build for the entirety of Mathlib, so it is doing a batch of refactoring in a Defs.lean or Basic.lean file, verifying that that file locally builds, then launches a lake build. Then it does more refactoring and spot fixing of any build errors, and launches another lake build. This basically allows one to advance one level up the Mathlib dependency tree every ten minutes or so. If you are curious, you can track the progress at https://github.com/teorth/mathlib4/tree/to_fun-refactor . I expect to be able to launch a PR within the hour.

I had initially asked the AI to grep for downstream usages to fix all at once, rather than rely on repeated waves of lake build to uncover the errors, but here I found that Mathlib's otherwise very convenient dot notation defeated this - there were way too many usages of, say, .inv throughout Mathlib to discern which ones were the ones that were impacted by the refactor and which ones were not. (Perhaps there are some Lean diagnostic tools that could trace this faster than performing a full build, but in any case I told the AI to just do waves of lake build followed by spot fixing the affected files, but this only lets me advance one layer of the dependency tree at a time, since lake refuses to build a file if one of its dependencies contains an error.)
A cool solution is to deprecate the lemmas you're looking for (@[deprecated "" (since := "")]) and then do a full build, then the log will tell you exactly where all the usages are
Yes, but this only extends as far as the lowest level of the dependency tree in which the lemma gets used. Any file downstream of that won't get built at all until that lower level gets fixed.

That's basically what we are using lake build for right now - as a blunt instrument to locate the lowest level dependencies. But I'm discovering that the dependency tree is deeper than expected. the AI right now is fixing a bunch of seventh-generation build errors in GelfandNaimarkSegal.lean, having fixed precursor errors in six previous levels already. (I would definitely not have volunteered for this refactor without modern AI assistance.)

Terence Tao said:

Any file downstream of that won't get built at all until that lower level gets fixed.

All the files will get built since there are no errors, just deprecation warnings
Which lines did it fixed? I'm looking at it (Mathlib/Analysis/CStarAlgebra/GelfandNaimarkSegal.lean)

Another way it could be done is the "Find all references" option command (which shows up when right-clicking a constant in VSCode): it shows you all places where this constant is used. This only works when you have all cache, and you haven't modified any of the other files (which would invalidate the cache). So, a possible approach would be to go through all theorems one by one, for each one using this trick to generate the fixes, and then git stash these fixes away, so that you still have valid cache. And then you can combine the stashes to get the final result without needing any lake build. However, this isn't super convenient either.

The advantage of the lake build approach here is that you only end up doing the changes that are actually necessary.

Nice! The AI added this to its "skill". There is still the MeasureTheory refactor to do, which I plan to make a separate PR for. Here things are slightly trickier because in many cases one has both a point-free and eta-expanded version, but with the "wrong" naming convention, e.g., docs#MeasureTheory.Integrable.sub and docs#MeasureTheory.Integrable.sub'. Doing the refactor would mean renaming .sub' to .fun_sub. I doubt many people will mourn the loss of the apostrophe version of the theorem, but it is sufficiently different that I wanted to postpone it to a separate PR. But with the new tricks suggested, it should go faster than the first one (now on depth 8).

Your AI setup may already have this all handled, but for future such refactors, there are some import graph DAG traversal scripts by @Kim Morrison and @Joachim Breitner in mathlib4's scripts/ directory which might be useful. See scripts/rm_set_option.py for an example for how they're used to remove "unnecessary" set_option lines efficiently.

How many batches have been planned for the to_fun-refactor branch?
The ninth build ended up causing no errors, and so I now have a PR which should hopefully pass CI: #40872

The refactor surfaced one quirk that maybe should be flagged for fun_prop maintainers: adding a new fun_prop lemma actually made fun_prop time out in one edge case, specifically at https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/40872/changes#diff-b89a3bf1a5d4a113024abc6f0e5bbc041ecf77d8fc5b4e9584e6a6c0967a3cbcL141 . The issue seems to be a notorious old problem, namely an instance diamond.

Here, the goal to be proven was

⊢ Continuous (fun a ↦ (m • (f.leftMulMapPreGNS x).completion) a)

Previously, this goal could be closed by fun_prop when the eta form Continuous (fun x ↦ c • g x) of Continuous.const_smul existed. The refactor added the point-free form Continuous (c • g), which created a unification issue for fun_prop. I will let the AI explain it below.

Content warning: AI-generated text

--
The crucial detail: m • (…).completion is scalar multiplication in the module of continuous linear maps — m • clm is itself a single CLM — not a pointwise Pi smul. Continuity of it is "a CLM is continuous," discharged in one step.

Why adding a lemma made it slower

fun_prop indexes its lemmas in a discrimination tree keyed on the head symbol of the conclusion's function.

Now the problem: the goal's m • clm also has head HSMul.hSMul — but via a completely different SMul instance (the CLM-module one) than the lemma's (Pi/pointwise). Head-symbol indexing can't tell the two instances apart, so the new point-free lemma becomes a candidate for this goal. To test the candidate, fun_prop must unify

m • clm     (CLM-module smul)   =?=   ?c • ?g   (Pi smul of a coerced function)

These are defeq only after pushing the coercion through (⇑(m • clm) = m • ⇑clm, coe_smul). To even discover that, the unifier has to whnf the goal's • to compare the two SMul instances — and that whnf descends into UniformSpace.Completion's smul, which is built from the heavy map/mulAux machinery (you can see the mulAux ↦ … (definition not exposed) note in the sibling errors). The normalization doesn't terminate within the 200 000-heartbeat budget → timeout.

So the chain is: new lemma → new candidate (head-symbol collision) → forced unification against a different instance → whnf of a computationally heavy Completion definition → heartbeat exhaustion.

Before the refactor there was no point-free const_smul lemma, so this candidate never existed; fun_prop went straight to the CLM-continuity discharger and never tried to whnf the Completion smul. The refactor's whole point was to make fun_prop stronger (match point-free goals) — but on this goal it strictly added a doomed, expensive unification attempt, turning a success into a timeout. Stronger in general, weaker here.
Is there a workaround for fun_prop that we could do directly then?

As you can see in the commit, the AI replaced the use of fun_prop here with a two-line term. The refactor was still a net size win (12 lines of code saved), but this was the one instance in all of Mathlib where the refactor actually made the code slightly longer. I don't fully understand the metaprogramming that is causing this issue, but it seems somewhat akin to fun_prop accidentally working previously due to something resembling defeq abuse, which got exposed by the refactor.
I'm trying to figure out the metaprogramming part of it as well, I have to investigate it further though.

To me, this points to fun_prop not respecting transparency enough, because as your LLM is pointing out fun a ↦ (m • (f.leftMulMapPreGNS x).completion) a) isn't of the form fun x ↦ c • g x.

I am one of the people that is a bit wary with all these duplicated lemmas. If our goal is to make fun_prop better, can't we just teach fun_prop to eta-expand any point-free statement (e.g. Continuous (f * g) -> Continuous (fun x => f x * g x))?

It could be implemented using something similar to eta_expand + simp only [mul_apply, add_apply, ...].

Well, even in that case, the refactor would be needed, because Mathlib currently only has the eta-expanded version. The refactor replaces those versions with the point-free version, and then also adds the to_fun attribute to automatically include the eta-expanded version. If fun_prop automatically did eta expansion then one might not need to add the to_fun tag, although there were dozens of other places outside of fun_prop where the eta-expanded version was used.

To reiterate, this refactor is not adding any new eta-expanded lemmas to Mathlib. It is adding point-free lemmas which previously only existed in Mathlib in eta-expanded form (and, concurrently, renaming some eta-expanded Mathlib lemmas).
What Floris means is that the fun_prop tactic would preprocess the goal so that it is in eta expanded form. Hence, we will only need a fun_prop tag on the eta expanded lemmas (which we already have)

If we would implement my suggestion we only need the eta-expanded version of the lemmas, not the eta-reduced version that is added in your PR. But we could also merge the PR as a stop-gap to the proper fix.
Is there a reason to only want the eta expanded versions? In rw, I sometimes build the side conditions by hand, and not having the syntactically correct lemma would make the rewrite fail

Oh yes, I've seen that as well, and I tend to mitigate this by using by exact so that it is only elaborated after the rewrite lemma is applied.

My only concern is lemma duplication. This is only a small cost with an attribute by to_fun, but I think it's still a cost.

There is indeed a small cost with the duplication, but IMHO the cost of not having the lemma available when you need it for a rewrite (of for current fun_prop) is much higher, so I'm definitely in favor of the PR.

Ok, that's fair.

I've bors merge'd Terry Tao's PR.

Made a second PR at #40872 to do a further round of to_fun'ing, mostly for the (AE)(Strongly)Measurable operations div, mul, smul, sup, inf and their to_additive components. In some cases, the eta-expanded and point-free versions both existed, but one of which had an ad hoc name such as docs#AEMeasurable.mul'. These versions are now deprecated in the PR (leading to a modest reduction in the codebase by about a dozen lines of code). A dozen or so downstream files needed minor edits to restore the build.

Note: the (AE)StronglyMeasurable lemmas such as docs#StronglyMeasurable.mul, in contrast to the others refactored here, were already in point-free form with no eta-expanded counterpart. For consistency, I (or more precisely, the AI agent I used) added the eta-expanded version via the to_fun tag, but some commenters here had expressed reservations about adding to the number of eta-expanded lemmas. I think both options here are defensible, but given that for instance docs#Continuous.mul already had the to_fun tag before either of my refactors, I think it is consistent to also add the tag to methods such as StronglyMeasurable.mul.
